chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
title: The Hardy Brothers show band and the theater circuit
summary: He worked in the Hardy Brothers band, led by Coleridge Davis, his first show band, and describes the Lafayette and Alhambra circuit and the tree of hope.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: -- and another house band I worked with steady there -- I worked in another big band in Washington -- was the Hardy Brothers. That was -- now, that was a good show band. They could -- on the stage they knew how to throw their horns up and down. They did the same routines like Lunceford did, but only this is way before Lunceford. They were doing these kinds of routines way back there then.
What were the Hardy Brothers first names?

Wesley Hardy was one, and I can't think of the other guy's name. Wesley was the thin one, then there's a fat one we called Horse. I never did know Horse's name. But these were the two Hardy Brothers. But they weren't the leaders of the band. The leader of the band was Coleridge Davis, piano player. He led the band and did the arrangements. But it was the Hardy Brothers band, but Coleridge, he seemed
to handle that money and do everything else. He did the hiring and firing, so -- but they use that name, the Hardy Brothers.

And this was a pretty good band. The Hardy Brothers had a pretty good -- not too many of the guys made big names for themselves. But it was a good band. It was a good show, and they were experienced. And we played that circuit of theaters that all the colored bands played then. We called it round the world circuit. Was the Lafayette Theater. This was before the Apollo Theater. Shiffman had another theater called the Lafayette Theater.

And then there was the Alhambra Theater too used to run before the Apollo, right on 125th Street, down the street from the Apollo. And the last one he had was the Apollo. But the first one he had was the Lafayette Theater. This was outside the Lafayette Theater on Seventh Avenue and 131st was what they called the tree of hope.

You'd go out there, you didn't have no job, and rub that tree. You're supposed to get a job. It's kind of absurd when you stop and think of it today.' But this is way back. This is days before I ever got with Earl Hines or any of these bands, and I was playing little bands like that.
